turn_text: I think it's very hard to predict. I'm a conservative when it comes to impeachment in the sense of, I go back to William Pitt Fessenden and the impeachment of Andrew Johnson. William Pitt Fessenden was a senator from Maine. It was one of the six Republicans who voted against the impeachment of Andrew Johnson. And basically on the premise that impeachment should not be used simply to change the government that you don't like. Andrew Johnson was a terrible president. But Fessenden saw at the time that to have voted for his impeachment because the Republicans who controlled Congress didn't like Johnson's policies, didn't like him as a person would be fundamentally changing our system of government. We'd become a parliamentary system where he had to have a vote of confidence. And I think that was exactly the right thing. The Constitution says impeachment is high crimes in misdemeanors. It's not, we don't like the president or we don't like his or her policies. And so, you know, unless, if the Mueller investigation comes up with some kind of really serious egregious smoking gun that constitutes a crime, that's a different situation. But I think elections are the best way to change politics in this country.

Now, speaking of the house and women in the house, we have Shelly Pingree in the first congressional district who is a candidate. I know you know personally and you adore us. And now she has a challenger in Marty Groman, who is an independent. And with all due respect, sir, I think it's safe to say that everyone who runs as an independent in Maine is trying to emulate your brand. They're trying to be the next Angus King. And I guess what I'm wondering is when I look at somebody like Marty Groman, who's running against Shelley, who's in my view, totally qualified for the position, does he have any duty not to run? and essentially take up a seat that a competent woman is filling right now?
